title: Has the Online Safety Act reduced illegal harms online?
label: 27 October 2026 · Illegal content duties
summary: The committee questioned four experts about whether the Online Safety Act (OSA) has reduced illegal online harms. Witnesses agreed the Act set useful standards but so far has not reduced most illegal harms because of weak enforcement, limited data access for researchers and safe harbour rules that let platforms avoid taking some measures. They urged better enforcement, clearer rules on platforms’ duties, improved data access, stronger prevention measures (including identity checks, hashing and upload prevention for encrypted services) and urgent action on AI risks.

glossary.definition: UK law that sets duties for tech companies to reduce online harms and to follow Ofcom's safety codes.
The UK communications regulator that enforces the Online Safety Act.
A legal rule in the OSA that can exempt platforms from extra duties if they follow the published codes.
A platform's written analysis of what illegal harms could happen on its service and how likely they are.
A technical method that blocks known illegal images or videos by comparing digital fingerprints.
A system where only sender and receiver can read messages, preventing servers (and often operators) from seeing content.
Tech that checks files before they are uploaded (even on encrypted apps) to stop known illegal material being shared.
A technical interface platforms provide so researchers or apps can access data; access to APIs affects the ability to study platforms.

chapters.title: Introductions and the question
chapters.takeaway: Four expert witnesses describe their focus: fraud, online harms research, terrorist misuse, and child sexual abuse material.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at the Online Safety Act’s impact on illegal content. Please introduce yourselves and your organisations.

turns.speaker: Rocio Concha
turns.text: I’m Rocio Concha from Which?. We focus on consumer harms and fraud and how the OSA affects those problems.

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: I’m Rys Farthing from Reset Tech; we research online hate, scams and cross-harm dynamics.

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: I’m Adam Hadley from Tech Against Terrorism; we study and disrupt terrorists’ use of the internet.

turns.speaker: Hannah Swirsky
turns.text: I’m Hannah Swirsky from the Internet Watch Foundation; we hunt and remove child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

chapters.title: Has the OSA reduced illegal harms?
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses agree the Act set standards but have seen little reduction in most illegal harms so far, citing weak enforcement and rising harm in several areas.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Has the Act reduced the harms each of you handles?

turns.speaker: Rocio Concha
turns.text: On fraud: no. User-generated scams have increased and Ofcom hasn’t enforced the fraud-related parts of the code. Rules about fraudulent advertising are delayed until mid-2027.

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: We’ve not seen hate speech or scam levels fall. Where regulation has been clear and enforced—like age checks for pornography—platforms changed. That shows enforcement matters.

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: For terrorist content there’s no evidence the OSA reduced availability. Big platforms aren’t consistently measurable and may be doing the minimum once codes exist.

turns.speaker: Hannah Swirsky
turns.text: CSAM is worsening—we processed a record number of reports last year. The Act did require hash matching and that can help, and some small services are using our free tools, but the problem keeps growing.

chapters.title: Data access and observability
chapters.takeaway: Research and regulation are hampered because researchers and regulators lack reliable access to platform data and APIs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What information is needed to tell if platforms are reducing illegal content, and do researchers have access?

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: Comprehensive data on content, reports, moderation and algorithmic amplification is needed. APIs that were once free are now limited or costly, and DCMS promises on data access haven’t been enacted yet.

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: We build crawlers for small platforms but large platforms block analysis with anti-bot measures and restrictive APIs—some forbid research use. Without researcher access or a regulator’s observability, you can’t measure compliance.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: So do you want new powers or new units to watch the internet?

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: Yes: a dedicated government unit to monitor the internet and open-source intelligence capability, plus legally enforceable researcher access like the EU’s DSA provides.

chapters.title: Safe harbour, risk assessments and enforcement
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses criticise safe harbour, argue platforms self-assess risk, and call for stronger enforcement and clearer duties rather than leaving mitigation optional.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: Ofcom has categorised services by size not risk, so only certain platforms must do full risk assessments—should the OSA be changed?

turns.speaker: Hannah Swirsky
turns.text: There’s a gap: platforms can claim mitigation isn’t ‘technically feasible’ and avoid action, so safe harbour needs review and Ofcom should publish how it judges technical feasibility.

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: Platforms are effectively marking their own homework. Some claim basic tech isn’t feasible even while using AI; there’s a will-versus-ability issue and a question of forcing investment in safety tech.

turns.speaker: Rocio Concha
turns.text: The Act places responsibility on Ofcom to define measures in codes, but platforms often know what’s feasible. We need Ofcom to challenge underestimates of risk and enforce codes, not just accept self-assessments.

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: A narrow legal fix could clarify that Ofcom must factor risk into categorisation and that platforms must act on the risks they identify, not treat codes as a ceiling that gives safe harbour.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Should we add a duty of care or similar to replace or sit above safe harbour?

turns.speaker: Rocio Concha
turns.text: I don’t want to delay current implementation; enforce what exists first, while debating safe harbour reforms in parallel.

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: You don’t need to scrap the Act—targeted reforms (remove safe harbour, require mitigation) could align practice with Parliament’s original intent.

chapters.title: Prevention, reporting and role of specialist organisations
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses want more proactive prevention measures—identity checks, stay-down, cross-platform blocking and better reporting—plus funding for civil society doing reporting work.

turns.speaker: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate
turns.text: Is prevention better than takedown? Are the codes strong enough for proactive measures?

turns.speaker: Rocio Concha
turns.text: Much action remains reactive. Ofcom’s upcoming decision on proactive technologies matters for fraud; proactive identity verification on dating and booking platforms would help.

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: Codes emphasise individual content removal (whack-a-mole) with no stay-down or systemic rules. We need rules on platform systems—terms, algorithmic promotion and business model effects—so harm isn't continually recreated.

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: For terrorism, content is cross-platform. We provide URL and hash lists, but big platforms often ignore referrals. Prevention needs platforms to stop recommending extremist content and use off-ramps and blocking where possible.

turns.speaker: Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge
turns.text: Are reporting systems any better? Who bears the burden of reporting?

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: Reporting flows are often user-unfriendly, asking people to make legal cases for moderators. Non-profits are doing large volumes of reporting pro bono while platforms and governments lack coordinated capacity.

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: We share hundreds of thousands of verified terrorist referrals; platforms largely ignore them. Governments in other countries (e.g., Australia) require platform cooperation and that has helped.

turns.speaker: Hannah Swirsky
turns.text: For CSAM hosted in the UK, takedowns work quickly with hosts; but platforms need to do more of the heavy lifting and financial institutions could be required to act when content is commercialised.

chapters.title: Encryption, AI risks and final priorities
chapters.takeaway: Experts press for upload-prevention on encrypted services, stronger AI safety measures (benchmarks, red-teaming, safety-by-design), and better enforcement and data for regulators.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Can technology check CSAM in end-to-end encrypted apps without breaking privacy?

turns.speaker: Hannah Swirsky
turns.text: Yes: 'upload prevention' can detect known CSAM before upload in privacy-preserving ways; it’s market-ready and should be required. Measures are needed on-device, at app-level and at ISPs.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: How should the OSA respond to generative AI creating or amplifying harms?

turns.speaker: Hannah Swirsky
turns.text: AI has multiplied harms like AI-generated CSAM; we need primary legislation for AI safety-by-design, plus the Crime and Policing Act measures operationalised quickly (nudification ban, red-teaming, chatbot scope).

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: AI misuse by terrorists and hostile states is a national security risk. Focus has been on existential 'misalignment' but not on misuse; we need safety benchmarks to measure how models respond to malicious queries.

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: Chatbots could be covered with a few targeted OSA reforms and stronger codes; regulation, industry measures and safety-by-design must work together.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: Has Ofcom’s enforcement driven major change?

turns.speaker: Hannah Swirsky
turns.text: There have been wins: some file-sharing sites were required to add hash matching and some porn sites improved age checks. But enforcement is patchy and Ofcom needs resources and clarity to prioritise.

turns.speaker: Rocio Concha
turns.text: From the fraud perspective, there’s little enforcement so far; private rights of action could help but only alongside stronger regulatory enforcement.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: If you could pick one practical change that would make the biggest difference, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Rocio Concha
turns.text: Fully enforce and implement the OSA now, while debating safe harbour reform in parallel.

turns.speaker: Dr Rys Farthing
turns.text: Remove safe harbour, require platforms to mitigate the risks in their risk assessments, and make codes less narrowly technical and more outcome-focused.

turns.speaker: Adam Hadley
turns.text: Create an online harms dashboard based on mandated data submissions (Section 154A type reporting) so everyone can see what’s on the internet and measure change.

turns.speaker: Hannah Swirsky
turns.text: Adopt a clear safety-by-design code, remove safe harbour problems, and use Section 121 powers to require technically feasible mitigation, including upload prevention in encrypted services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We’ll follow up on technical details, enforcement and AI in our report. We appreciate your evidence and time today.
